questions.question: An artist presents a work that consists only of a written set of instructions, producing no physical object. Based on the article's description, this work is best understood as an example of which category?
options: Conceptual art
Ceramic art
Photography
Applied art
answer_explanations: Correct. The article defines conceptual art as art 'where the concepts or ideas involved in the work take precedence over traditional aesthetic and material concerns,' presenting idea-based art 'as text.' A instructions-only work with no object fits this description.
Incorrect. Ceramic art is made from ceramic materials such as pottery, tiles, and figurines; it is a material, object-based practice.
Incorrect. Photography is a visual art centred on photographs, not on ideas expressed as text.
Incorrect. Applied art applies design and decoration to functional objects, which still requires a physical object.

questions.question: A composer writes a piece in which performers improvise freely within a loose structure. According to the article's discussion of the performing arts, how is this work best classified?
options: As an improvised work, since performing-arts products can be improvised rather than repeatable
As a visual art, because a stage is involved
As literature, because the instructions are written down
As an applied art, because it serves a practical function
answer_explanations: Correct. The article says performing-arts products are 'broadly categorized as being either repeatable (for example, by script or score) or improvised for each performance.' Free improvisation fits the improvised category.
Incorrect. A stage setting does not make a work a visual art; the article places music in the performing arts.
Incorrect. Being written down does not make a work literature; the article treats music as a performing art, and notes literature is about artistic linguistic expression.
Incorrect. Applied art concerns the design of functional objects, not musical performance.

questions.question: A sculptor stops carving marble and instead welds and moulds found metal objects. The article presents this kind of shift as characteristic of what?
options: Modernism's expansion of sculptural materials and processes
The rejection of sculpture as a visual art
A return to Ancient Greek proportions
The decline of the plastic arts
answer_explanations: Correct. The article says 'shifts in sculptural processes have led to almost complete freedom of materials and processes following modernism,' with materials assembled by welding or modelling, or moulded or cast.
Incorrect. The article keeps sculpture within the visual arts; it does not describe it as being rejected.
Incorrect. Free use of materials is a modernist development, not a return to Greek conventions of proportion.
Incorrect. The article names sculpture 'one of the plastic arts' and describes its expansion, not its decline.

questions.question: The article notes that 'drama is literature with acting' and 'dance is music expressed through motion.' What broader point do these examples support?
options: That some arts are derived from or combine other arts, so the categories interweave
That literature is superior to music
That dance is not a performing art
That the Seven Arts are entirely independent of one another
answer_explanations: Correct. The article uses these examples to show that 'some arts may be derived from others,' and that art forms can 'combine and interweave' rather than stay separate.
Incorrect. The examples describe combinations, not a ranking of one art above another.
Incorrect. Dance is explicitly listed as a performing art; the point is its relationship to music.
Incorrect. These examples demonstrate the opposite — that the arts are interconnected and can be derived from one another.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the article's position on the debate over whether video games are art?
options: Video games contain artistic elements and have won institutional recognition, yet their status remains debated by creators and commentators
Video games are universally accepted as the highest form of art
Video games are strictly a science and have no artistic elements
The debate was settled in 2006 when Hideo Kojima called video games art
answer_explanations: Correct. The article describes video games as having 'uncontroversial artistic elements such as visuals and sound,' notes ongoing debates over classifying them as art, and records institutional recognition such as the NEA's 2011 inclusion of video games as a 'work of art' and the Smithsonian's 2012 exhibit.
Incorrect. The article stresses that the status of video games remains debated, not universally agreed.
Incorrect. The article acknowledges clear artistic elements in video games, so this overstates the case against them.
Incorrect. Kojima argued in 2006 that video games are 'a type of service rather than an art form' — the opposite of this statement.

questions.question: A government funds a nationwide mural campaign promoting its policies. Using the article's terms, which relationship does this most directly illustrate?
options: The use of art as propaganda to promote a government agenda
The complete separation of art from politics
The classification of murals as performing arts
The idea that art criticism determines an artwork's value
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that 'Governments use art, or propaganda, to promote their own agendas,' and that art can take on political dimensions as it responds to news and politics.
Incorrect. This scenario shows a tight link between art and politics, not a separation.
Incorrect. Murals are visual works, not performing arts, which require a live performance.
Incorrect. The scenario concerns government promotion, not the role of critics.

questions.question: What does the article imply about the long-term reliability of art criticism?
options: Critics' judgments can be revised over time, and past critics have been ridiculed for dismissing artists now venerated
Art criticism is an exact science whose verdicts are permanent
Critics are always correct about the art of their own time
Art criticism has no connection to aesthetics or the theory of beauty
answer_explanations: Correct. The article notes that 'opinions of current art are liable to corrections with the passage of time' and that 'critics of the past can be ridiculed for dismissing artists now venerated (like the early work of the Impressionists).'
Incorrect. The article presents criticism as revisable, not as exact or permanent.
Incorrect. The Impressionist example shows critics can be wrong about the art of their own time.
Incorrect. The article explicitly links art criticism to aesthetics, the theory of beauty.

questions.question: A museum decides to exhibit only objects that are beautiful or intellectually stimulating but serve no everyday function. Which distinction from the article is the museum applying?
options: The distinction between fine art and applied art
The distinction between painting and sculpture
The distinction between historical and contemporary criticism
The distinction between music and dance
answer_explanations: Correct. The article defines fine art as producing objects that are beautiful or provide intellectual stimulation but have 'no primary everyday function,' contrasted with applied art, which decorates functional objects.
Incorrect. Painting and sculpture are both forms of fine/visual art, so this distinction does not match.
Incorrect. Historical versus contemporary criticism concerns the timing of criticism, not the function of objects.
Incorrect. Music and dance are performing arts; they are not divided by everyday function.

questions.question: Based on the article, why might it be difficult to draw a firm line between 'art' and 'craft'?
options: Because the arts span everyday practices and are continually redefined, and categories like the applied arts overlap with fine art
Because craft was banned throughout the Middle Ages
Because only painting is truly considered an art
Because craft is actually a branch of mathematics
answer_explanations: Correct. The article says the arts include everyday practices, that 'the arts themselves are open to being continually redefined,' and that in practice fine art and applied art 'often overlap.' Together these blur any firm art/craft line.
Incorrect. The article does not say craft was banned; it links art and craft historically through techne.
Incorrect. The article recognizes many arts beyond painting — visual, literary, and performing.
Incorrect. Mathematics relates to the historical quadrivium, not to craft as such.

questions.question: The article says performing-arts products are either 'repeatable (for example, by script or score) or improvised.' Which example best matches a 'repeatable' product as defined there?
options: A play performed night after night from a script
A jazz solo invented in the moment of performance
A sculpture carved from a block of stone
A photograph taken by a photojournalist
answer_explanations: Correct. The article gives 'script or score' as examples of repeatable performing-arts products, so a scripted play staged repeatedly fits.
Incorrect. A solo invented in the moment is the article's example of the improvised category, not the repeatable one.
Incorrect. A sculpture is a visual-art object, not a performing-arts product, so the repeatable/improvised distinction does not apply.
Incorrect. A photograph is a visual-art object and is not a performed product at all.
